title: Race to the Finish Line
summary: A boy who is always the slowest runner on his school team learns pacing and steady breathing from his coach, and after weeks of practice, beats his own best time at the final school track meet.
poll: Beating your own best time matters more than winning a race.

versions.title: Race to the Finish Line
versions.text:
Zaid runs on his school team. He likes to race. But he is slow. He comes in last each time.

Zaid feels sad about this. He wants to be fast. His coach sees him. His coach is Coach Ali.

Coach Ali has two tips. First, do not run too fast at the start. Save your strength. Second, breathe slow and deep.

Zaid tries the tips. He runs each day after school. He runs for many weeks.

Each week, Zaid gets a bit faster. He does not win. But his time gets better each week.

Then the big race comes. It is the last race of the year. Zaid lines up. He does not look at the other kids.

He breathes slow. He keeps a good pace. He runs his own race.

Zaid does not win. But he beats his own best time! Coach Ali is proud. His team is proud too.

Zaid learns a big thing. To get better than before is a win too.

versions.title: Race to the Finish Line
versions.text:
Zaid runs on his school's race team, and he truly loves to race. But he is not a fast runner, and he comes in last in almost every single race.

This makes Zaid feel quite sad and a bit shy around his friends. He does not like coming in last again and again. His coach notices how sad Zaid feels after each race. His coach is named Coach Ali.

One day, Coach Ali sits with Zaid and gives him two simple tips. First, Zaid should not run too fast at the very start of a race, since that wastes his strength early on. Second, he should breathe in a slow, steady way the whole time he runs.

Zaid decides to try out these new tips. He runs every day after school, rain or shine. He keeps this up for many weeks in a row, even when he feels tired.

Week by week, Zaid starts to notice that he is getting a little faster. He still does not win any of the small races. But his own running time keeps getting better each week.

At last, the big school race comes. It is the final race of the whole school year. Zaid lines up at the starting line. He does not look at the other runners beside him.

Instead, he breathes slow and steady. He keeps a good, even pace the whole way. He simply runs his own race, just like his coach taught him.

Zaid does not win that day, and that feels okay. But he beats his own best time ever, by a few seconds! Coach Ali claps loudly for him, and his whole team cheers too.

Zaid learns something important that day. Getting better than you were before can feel just like winning.

One afternoon, Coach Ali sits with Zaid and shares two helpful tips. First, do not sprint at full speed at the very start, because that wastes strength too soon. Second, breathe in a slow, steady rhythm the whole time.

Zaid decides to try both tips that same day. He runs every afternoon after school. He keeps this up for several weeks in a row. He does this even when his legs feel tired.

Week by week, Zaid starts to feel stronger. He still does not win any small race. But his own running time keeps getting better.

Finally, the big school track meet arrives. The whole school feels excited. Zaid lines up at the start and takes a deep breath. He does not look at the runners near him.

Instead, he breathes slowly. He keeps a steady pace the whole way. He focuses only on his own race.

Zaid does not win the race that day, and that feels okay. He crosses the line with his very best time ever. Coach Ali claps proudly, and the whole team cheers.

Zaid learns something important that day. Getting better than before can feel just as good as winning.

versions.title: Race to the Finish Line
versions.text:
Zaid has always loved running. But speed has never come easily to him. He runs on his school's race team. Every week, the team runs a short race. Almost every time, Zaid finishes last, no matter how hard he tries.

This pattern leaves Zaid feeling discouraged and a little embarrassed. He does not enjoy finishing last again and again. His coach, Coach Ali, notices his discouraged face after each race. Coach Ali has trained young runners for many years.

One afternoon after practice, Coach Ali sits with Zaid. He shares two useful tips about racing wisely. First, do not sprint at full speed at the very start. That quickly uses up the strength needed later. Second, breathe in a slow, steady rhythm instead of gasping for air.

Zaid decides to try out both tips that same day. He runs every afternoon after school. It does not matter if it is sunny or rainy. He keeps this routine going for several weeks in a row, even when his legs feel tired.

Week by week, Zaid notices that he is slowly becoming stronger. He still does not manage to win any small practice race. However, his own personal time keeps improving each week.

Finally, the big school track meet arrives. The whole school feels excited about this final race of the year. Zaid lines up at the start of the four-hundred-meter race. He takes a deep breath and deliberately avoids looking at the runners speeding past him.

Instead, he breathes slowly. He keeps a steady pace the whole way, exactly how his coach taught him. He focuses only on his own race.

Zaid does not win the race that afternoon. Surprisingly, that feels completely fine. He crosses the finish line with his very own best time ever, beating his old record by several seconds. Coach Ali claps loudly and proudly, and the whole team cheers with excitement.

Zaid finally understands something important that day. Becoming better than you used to be can feel every bit as good as winning first place.

versions.title: Race to the Finish Line
versions.text:
Running has never come naturally or effortlessly to Zaid, despite years of persistent trying, and yet he genuinely loves the sport regardless of how unkindly it often treats him in competition. As a member of his school's race team, he competes weekly in a short race, and almost without exception, he finishes last among his teammates, regardless of how diligently he trains beforehand or how determined he feels standing at the starting line.

This repeated, discouraging pattern leaves Zaid feeling embarrassed in front of classmates who rarely notice the quiet, persistent effort behind his ongoing struggle, since finishing last offers no visible reward. He takes no pleasure whatsoever in losing race after race while faster runners celebrate enthusiastically around him, and his coach, Coach Ali, eventually notices the toll this pattern is taking and decides that passive observation from the sidelines is no longer an acceptable response.

One afternoon, Coach Ali sits beside Zaid and explains two essential concepts regarding pacing: a runner should never expend maximum effort during the opening stretch of a race, since doing so rapidly depletes the endurance and stamina the body will urgently require during the later, more demanding portions of the course, and a runner should instead maintain a slow, steady breathing rhythm throughout, rather than gasping unpredictably whenever fatigue sets in.

Resolving to practice daily regardless of exhaustion or motivation, Zaid continues training for several consecutive weeks, enduring both pleasant and unpleasant weather without skipping a single session, and concentrating each time on applying both techniques simultaneously as though following a well-tested formula refined through years of coaching experience. Gradually, he begins noticing genuine, measurable improvement in his performance and in his own growing self-confidence, even though he still fails to win any of the practice races against his teammates throughout this extended stretch of training; nevertheless, his personal time keeps dropping steadily with every week of consistent, deliberate effort.

When the major school track meet finally arrives, the entire school feels genuine excitement about this final athletic event of the year. Zaid lines up for the four-hundred-meter race, takes a calming breath to settle his nerves, and deliberately refuses to glance at the runners sprinting ahead of him, keeping his attention focused firmly inward rather than comparing himself to others. Rather than panicking under pressure, he breathes slowly and sustains an even pace throughout, exactly as his coach had patiently taught him across many weeks of practice together.

Zaid does not win the race that afternoon, and surprisingly, this outcome proves entirely acceptable, even genuinely welcome, to him. He crosses the finish line having achieved his own personal best time, beating his previous record by several seconds through sheer perseverance and discipline, and Coach Ali claps proudly as the entire team cheers, finally recognizing his quiet, determined effort. Zaid finally grasps that becoming better than one used to be can feel every bit as rewarding as winning outright, and perhaps even more meaningful, since that kind of victory belongs entirely to the person who earned it through their own sustained effort over time.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?

A boy who gets better at running by practicing
A boy who bakes bread for his team
A boy who wins every single race

questions.stem: What two tips does Coach Ali give Zaid?

options: Coach Ali stops coaching the team
Zaid wins a small practice race
Zaid stops running completely

questions.stem: Why does Zaid's running time get better each week?

He practices and uses his coach's tips
He eats more candy

questions.stem: How does Zaid most likely feel when he beats his own best time?

Angry and upset

the fastest time he has ever run
the only time he has ever run

wrong.C: Zaid has run many races, not just one.
wrong.D: Best means fastest, not slowest, for a runner.

options: To explain that running races is a bad idea
To make readers feel sad for Zaid
To show that winning is the only thing that matters
To show that getting better than before can feel like winning too
questions.why: The story ends with Zaid learning that beating his own best time felt like a win, even without first place.

wrong.A: The article shows running helps Zaid, not that it is bad.
wrong.B: The ending is happy, not sad.

LOW.prompt: Do you think Zaid's race was a success, even though he did not win? Explain your answer using at least two facts from the article.

I used at least two facts from the article.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: I think Zaid's race was a success. He practiced every day for many weeks and used his coach's tips about pacing and breathing. Even though he did not win the race, he beat his own best time by several seconds. That shows he really improved, so I think his race was a success.

keyWords.definition: the speed at which someone moves or does something

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the article?

wrong.C: This is the opposite of the coach's advice.

Just one short afternoon of practice
Several weeks in a row, almost every day

Zaid quietly quits the school running team

questions.stem: Why does Zaid's personal running time keep improving each week?

He simply stops attending school for a while
questions.why: Zaid's steady practice, combined with the pacing and breathing tips, causes his personal time to keep getting better.

wrong.B: The article does not mention racing younger students.

questions.stem: In the article, the word discouraged means —
options: extremely proud of a recent achievement
feeling like giving up because something is hard
completely confused about a school lesson

questions.why: Zaid feels discouraged because he keeps finishing last, which means he feels like giving up.

questions.stem: Why does Coach Ali most likely decide to talk with Zaid about pacing?

questions.stem: How does the author organize events in this article?

By describing a school race that never actually happens
By listing several facts about running shoes
By showing Zaid's struggle, the coach's tips, weeks of practice, then the race

wrong.A: Only one coach, Coach Ali, appears in the article.

wrong.C: The article does not describe running shoes.

MID.prompt: Explain how Coach Ali's two tips helped Zaid improve. Use at least two details from the article.
checklist: I explained how the tips helped Zaid.
I used at least two details from the article.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: Coach Ali's two tips helped Zaid become a better runner. First, Coach Ali told Zaid not to sprint at the very start, so Zaid would not waste his strength too early in the race. Second, Coach Ali told Zaid to breathe in a slow, steady rhythm, which helped him stay calm instead of gasping for air. Zaid practiced these tips every day for several weeks, and his personal running time kept getting better because of them.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?

HIGH.prompt: Do you agree that becoming better than you once were can feel just as rewarding as winning outright? Support your position with evidence from the article about Zaid's experience.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the prompt.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the article.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that becoming better than you once were can feel just as rewarding as winning outright. Zaid's experience shows this clearly: he trained with consistent effort for several weeks, applying Coach Ali's pacing and breathing techniques, and he finished the big race by beating his own personal best time through sheer perseverance, even though he did not come in first place. Someone might argue that only first place truly counts in competition, but Zaid's steady improvement in endurance and stamina, built through weeks of consistent practice, represents a genuine personal achievement that no single race result could fully capture.
